title: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (CST): A Critical Ophthalmic Emergency
summary: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis is a rare, life-threatening condition characterized by a blood clot within the cavernous sinus, often resulting from spreading infections. Rapid identification of ocular and neurological signs is vital for survival and vision preservation.

sections.title: Understanding Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis
sections.content: Cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST) is the formation of a blood clot within the cavernous sinus, a large dural venous sinus located at the base of the skull. This condition is most commonly caused by the retrograde spread of infection from the 'danger triangle' of the face, the paranasal sinuses, or the teeth. Because the veins of the face lack valves, bacteria can travel backward into the cavernous sinus, leading to inflammation, thrombus formation, and potential damage to the vital cranial nerves that pass through it.

sections.title: Anatomical Contents of the Cavernous Sinus
Clinical Signs & Symptoms
content: Abrupt onset of unilateral periorbital edema and chemosis
Proptosis (bulging of the eye) due to venous congestion
Ophthalmoplegia: Paralysis of eye muscles (CN III, IV, VI)
Severe headache or retro-orbital pain
Decreased corneal sensation (CN V1 involvement)
Fever, chills, and altered mental status (Systemic involvement)
Bilateral progression: Signs usually spread to the other eye within 24-48 hours

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Act Immediately
content: Rapidly progressing bilateral proptosis
Complete external ophthalmoplegia (frozen eye)
Papilledema or retinal vein engorgement
Signs of meningitis (nuchal rigidity, Kernig's sign)
Sepsis or septic shock indicators

sections.title: Diagnostic & Management Pathway
content: Step 1: Clinical Suspicion - Immediate neurological and ophthalmic exam.
Step 2: Imaging - MRI with MRV (preferred) or Contrast-enhanced CT to visualize filling defects.
Step 3: Laboratory Work - Blood cultures, CBC, and Lumbar Puncture if meningitis is suspected.
Step 4: Aggressive Antibiotics - High-dose IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone/Metronidazole).
Step 5: Anticoagulation - Consider Heparin to prevent thrombus propagation.
Step 6: Surgical Intervention - Drainage of the primary infection source (e.g., sinus surgery).

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Mortality rate: Reduced to <20% with modern antibiotics
Vision loss (30% of survivors)
Persistent CN palsies
Pituitary insufficiency
Brain abscess or Meningitis

content.explanation: CN 6 is inside (with ICA), while CN 3, 4, 5 (V1/V2) are in the lateral wall. If CN 6 goes first, suspect CST early!
